claims.text: Conventional W–Cu metal-matrix composites have a distinct, sharp interface between tungsten and copper phases.
A sub-100 nm VFeTiTaW-based refractory high-entropy-alloy interlayer can be deposited at the W–Cu interface by sputtering or controlled diffusion bonding.
VFeTiTaW is a refractory high-entropy alloy investigated for fusion-relevant thermal and irradiation resistance.
The proposed interlayer will produce a graded interfacial region between tungsten and copper.
The graded region will bridge lattice mismatch between tungsten and copper.
The graded region will bridge acoustic-impedance mismatch between tungsten and copper.
Bridging the interfacial mismatches will reduce interfacial thermal resistance and phonon scattering.
Reduced interfacial phonon scattering will increase the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
VFeTiTaW has sufficient intrinsic high-temperature and irradiation stability for the proposed interlayer role.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit high thermal stability and resistance to irradiation-induced defect evolution.
The interlayer's refractory character and irradiation tolerance will preserve the W–Cu composite's mechanical integrity under extreme conditions.
The interlayer will increase effective thermal conductivity by 10–20% relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite without the interlayer.
Mechanical strength will remain comparable to or better than that of the baseline W–Cu composite.
Irradiation resistance will remain comparable to or better than that of the baseline W–Cu composite.
High thermal flux, elevated temperature, and irradiation are relevant operating conditions for fusion-reactor tungsten–copper joints.
The benefits require the interlayer to remain ultrathin and continuous.
Excessive interlayer thickness or poor compositional control may introduce defects and negate the improvements.
The exact conductivity improvement and long-term irradiation behavior are uncertain and sensitive to interlayer uniformity and processing.
Failure to achieve at least a 10% conductivity increase, or significant loss of mechanical or irradiation performance, is defined to falsify the hypothesis.
